title: Single-use state transitions under concurrency and replay

threat_model.actor: Any caller able to issue the same logical request twice, including an automatic client retry, a proxy, a queue, or a provider redelivery
threat_model.asset: Single-use resources and exactly-once side effects such as vouchers, invitations, seats, quotas, and outbound charges
threat_model.trust_boundary: Observed resource state to the write that consumes it
threat_model.failure_mode: A check-then-act sequence reads an unconsumed state and commits the consumption in a separate, unserialized step
threat_model.impact: Two or more executions each observe the resource as available, so a single-use resource is consumed repeatedly or an external side effect is duplicated

required_evidence: A resource or side effect is intended to occur at most once per logical identifier
The same operation can be triggered concurrently or repeated by a client retry, proxy replay, queue redelivery, or provider callback

signals: A read that establishes a consumed flag is followed by a separate write that sets it
The mutating statement carries no conditional predicate, row lock, or unique constraint expressing the precondition
The configured isolation level is weaker than the serializable behaviour the code assumes
A request that causes an external effect accepts no idempotency key, or accepts one with no uniqueness constraint behind it
A retry policy exists in the client, gateway, or mesh while the server treats every attempt as a new request
A queue or webhook handler applies an event without recording the event id as consumed
Delivery is at-least-once by design while the handler is written as if it were exactly-once
A voucher redemption reads the redeemed field and updates it in a second statement
A charge helper checks a processed marker before calling the provider and writes it afterwards

boundary.subject: the execution attempting the transition, identified by its logical request
boundary.object: a resource whose consumed state may change at most once
boundary.invariant: At most one execution may commit the consumption, and every repeat of the same logical request converges on that first committed outcome

signals: Locate every read that establishes a precondition and check whether the dependent write re-asserts that precondition in its own predicate
Follow the transaction boundary: where it opens, where it commits, and whether the precondition read sits inside it
Identify the replay sources above the handler — client libraries, gateways, queues, provider redelivery — that can repeat one logical request
State the correct outcome of two simultaneous identical requests, then ask whether the code can produce any other outcome
Separate at-most-once from at-least-once: an external effect needs a durable claim before the effect and a durable record after it
Enumerate the outcome-unknown states — timeout, crash between effect and record — and decide what the next attempt must do
Check for a unique constraint or primary key that would make the duplicate physically impossible regardless of application code
Check the deployed isolation level against the guarantees the code depends on
Check whether the idempotency key is stable across attempts of one logical request or regenerated per attempt
Release identical executions from one barrier against an isolated fixture and count committed transitions and recorded side effects
Repeat the same logical request after an injected timeout or a simulated crash between the effect and its record, then count again

steps: Confirm explicit authorization and build an isolated fixture whose provider stub counts side effects instead of causing them
Record the single-execution baseline so a concurrent result can be compared with a known-good outcome
Release several identical executions from a shared barrier and count committed transitions and recorded side effects
Repeat the request after an injected timeout or simulated crash between the effect and its record, then count again
Record the isolation level, the guarding predicate, and the observed counts without using production credentials or live provider endpoints

false_positive_filters: A unique constraint, primary key, or conditional update already makes the second commit impossible and the code merely reports the failure poorly
The provider enforces idempotency on the key it receives, and the evidence shows that key is derived per logical request rather than per attempt
The resource is single-writer by construction, for example a partitioned consumer holding an exclusive lease
The duplicate effect is naturally idempotent, for example a write that sets a field to a constant value
An upstream serializing lock is evidenced, so the window is not reachable from a caller-controlled entrypoint

required_evidence: The precondition read and the dependent write quoted together with the transaction and isolation context between them
Evidence that one logical request can be executed twice, whether by the caller, a retry layer, or a redelivery
A safe isolated reproduction counting more than one committed consumption or side effect for one logical request
The concrete impact of the duplicate: value moved twice, quota bypassed, or an exactly-once contract broken downstream
refutation_tests: Inspect the schema and migrations for unique constraints, and the query for conditional predicates that would collapse the race independent of application code
Run the same reproduction against a known-correct path to confirm the harness can tell a real duplicate from a flaky fixture
Vary the duplication vector across concurrency, retry, and redelivery, since a control against one does not imply a control against the others
Check whether the downstream provider deduplicates on a key that is stable across attempts before treating the duplicate as reachable

root_causes: Check-then-act: the precondition is evaluated in application memory and the committing write never re-asserts it
The idempotency record is written after the external effect, leaving a window in which the effect exists and the record does not
The idempotency key is derived per attempt rather than per logical request, so retries present as new requests
The code assumes serializable isolation while the deployment runs a weaker default
Uniqueness is enforced only by an application-level lookup with no constraint in the store
Timeout and crash are treated as failure, so the next attempt repeats an effect that already succeeded

variant_strategy.result_contract: EXACT | VARIANT | REFUTED | BLOCKED; exact and variant matches remain hypotheses until verified

remediation.canonical_invariant: Make the precondition part of the committing write — a conditional update, a unique constraint, or a claim row — and decide the outcome from that write's own result
patterns: Claim first, act second, finalize last: write a claim keyed by the logical request before causing an external effect and complete it afterwards
Carry the precondition in the write predicate and treat the affected-row count as the authoritative decision
Back every idempotency key with a unique constraint so duplicates are rejected by the store rather than by a prior read
Derive the idempotency key from the logical request so every retry reuses it, and forward that key to the downstream provider
Model timeout and crash as an explicit outcome-unknown state reconciled against the provider instead of retried blindly
Where an effect cannot be made idempotent, serialize on a lease or a single-consumer partition and document the throughput cost

assertions: The vulnerable voucher variant lets two concurrent redemptions both observe an unredeemed voucher and both credit a wallet
The remediated voucher variant claims with a conditional update so exactly one concurrent caller succeeds
The vulnerable charge variant calls the provider twice when the same request is retried before its record is durable
The remediated charge variant holds an idempotency claim and returns the first committed result on retry
Remediated variants still complete the first legitimate execution, so a blanket denial cannot pass as a fix

calibration.notes: This pack has not completed a reproducible benchmark run and makes no precision or recall claim.

limitations: A negative concurrency reproduction is weak evidence: the window may exist and simply be hard to hit on the test machine
Fixture timing does not represent production scheduling, connection pooling, or database isolation defaults
Store-level constraints often live in migrations that are not visible from the reviewed code path
Idempotency correctness ultimately depends on downstream provider semantics that this pack cannot establish
